results.title: The influence of upwelling on key bivalves from the Humboldt and Iberian current systems - ScienceDirect
results.content: # The influence of upwelling on key bivalves from the Humboldt and Iberian current systems. The influence of upwelling conditions was assessed on bivalve traits from the Humboldt and Iberian current systems. Water from upwelling sites had lower temperature and pH and higher nitrite content than downwelling sites at both systems. Mussels morphometric, organic content, and mechanical properties were also of better quality in upwelling sites. Mussels from upwelling sites showed consistently better conditions than those from downwelling in both systems. Eastern Boundary Upwelling Systems (EBUS) deliver cold, nutrient-rich waters, influencing coastal biota from the molecular to the ecosystem level. Although local upwelling (U) and downwelling (DU) conditions are often known, their influence on body attributes of relevant species has not been systematically compared within and between EBUS (i.e., below and above regional scales). Hence, we compared the physical-chemical characteristics of U and DU sites in the Humboldt Current system (Chile) and the Iberian Current system (Portugal). We then assessed the influence of U and DU upon eight body attributes in purple mussels (*Perumytilus purpuratus*) and Mediterranean mussels (*Mytilus galloprovincialis*), from the Humboldt and Iberian systems, respectively. We hypothesized that bivalves from U sites display better fitness, as measured by body attributes, regardless of their origin (EBUS). As expected, waters from U sites in both systems showed lower temperatures and pH, and higher nitrite concentrations. We also found that mussels from U sites showed better fitness than those in DU sites in 12 out of 16 direct U vs DU comparisons. Shell length, shell volume, organic content of soft-tissues, and mechanical properties of the shell averaged consistently higher in mussels from U sites in both Current systems. In addition, total weight, soft-tissue weight, shell weight and shell thickness were all higher in the U site at the Humboldt system but had less consistent differences at the Iberian system. Altogether, most results supported our working hypothesis and indicate that U conditions support better fitted mussels. The few attributes that did not exhibit the expected U vs DU differences in the Iberian system suggest that local and species-specific differences also play a role on the attributes of these species. ## Data availability. results.title: Replaying failed tests - Hypothesis 6.146.0 documentation
results.content: Replaying failures found by your Hypothesis tests is almost as important as finding failures in the first place. Hypothesis therefore contains several ways to replay failures: they are automatically saved to (and replayed from) a local `ExampleDatabase`, and can be manually replayed via `@example` or `@reproduce_failure`. ## The Hypothesis database¶. When a test fails, Hypothesis automatically saves the failure so it can be replayed later. import time from hypothesis import strategies as st @given(st. When Hypothesis saw the failure the first time, it automatically saved that failing input. On future runs, Hypothesis retries any failing inputs (in `Phase.explain`) before generating new inputs (in `Phase.generate`). Hypothesis saves failures to the `settings.database` setting. If you want Hypothesis to always run a specific input, you can use `@example`. `@example` adds an explicit input which Hypothesis will run every time, in addition to the randomly generated examples. Hypothesis runs all explicit examples first, in the `Phase.explicit` phase, before generating additional random examples in the `Phase.generate` phase. Note that unlike examples generated by Hypothesis, examples provided using `@example` do not shrink. Hypothesis will print `Falsifying explicitexample:test_something_with_integers(n=131071)`, instead of shrinking to `n=100`. If you want to ensure an input is run every time, use `@example`. ## Replaying examples with `@reproduce_failure`¶. If `settings.print_blob` is set to `True` (the default in the `ci` settings profile), and a test fails, Hypothesis will print an `@reproduce_failure` decorator containing an opaque blob as part of the error message:. assert f == f...>>> test()...Falsifying example: test( f=nan,)You can reproduce this example by temporarily adding @reproduce_failure('6.131.23', b'ACh/+AAAAAAAAA==') as a decorator on your test case. You can add this decorator to your test to reproduce the failure. If you work with multiple developers, or want to share failures across environments (such as locally replaying a failure found by CI), another option is to share the Hypothesis database. For instance, by setting `settings.database` to an instance of a networked database like `RedisExampleDatabase`, any developer connecting to that networked database will automatically replay any failures found by other developers. Similarly, setting `settings.database` to `GitHubArtifactDatabase` will automatically replay any failures found by the connected CI artifact.

results.title: Language adaptation and learning: Getting explicit about implicit learning | Max Planck Institute
results.content: ## Breadcrumb. ## Language adaptation and learning: Getting explicit about implicit learning. Chang, F., Janciauskas, M., & Fitz, H. Language adaptation and learning: Getting explicit about implicit learning. Language and Linguistics Compass, 6, 259-278. doi:10.1002/lnc3.337. Linguistic adaptation is a phenomenon where language representations change in response to linguistic input. Adaptation can occur on multiple linguistic levels such as phonology (tuning of phonotactic constraints), words (repetition priming), and syntax (structural priming). The persistent nature of these adaptations suggests that they may be a form of implicit learning and connectionist models have been developed which instantiate this hypothesis. Research on implicit learning, however, has also produced evidence that explicit chunk knowledge is involved in the performance of these tasks. In this review, we examine how these interacting implicit and explicit processes may change our understanding of language learning and processing. results.content: # Drift-Barrier Hypothesis: A Quantitative Genetics Guide. The Drift-Barrier Hypothesis is a fundamental concept in quantitative genetics that explains the role of genetic drift in shaping the evolution of populations. The hypothesis proposes that genetic drift acts as a barrier to the fixation of beneficial mutations, thereby influencing the efficacy of natural selection. The Drift-Barrier Hypothesis was first introduced by 1 as a way to understand the limitations of natural selection in shaping the evolution of complex traits. The hypothesis is based on the idea that genetic drift, which is the random change in allele frequencies in a population, can act as a barrier to the fixation of beneficial mutations. The Drift-Barrier Hypothesis is crucial in quantitative genetics because it helps to explain the observed patterns of genetic variation in populations. The Drift-Barrier Hypothesis is composed of several key components that work together to shape the evolution of populations. The interaction between genetic drift and natural selection is a critical component of the Drift-Barrier Hypothesis. The Drift-Barrier Hypothesis suggests that genetic drift can limit the efficacy of natural selection, leading to reduced adaptation in complex traits. The hypothesis also suggests that genetic drift can reduce the efficacy of natural selection, making it more difficult for beneficial mutations to become fixed in a population. The Drift-Barrier Hypothesis can influence the genetic architecture of populations by shaping the distribution of allele frequencies. Empirical evidence for the Drift-Barrier Hypothesis comes from studies of genetic variation in natural populations.
